item.title: Emergency water deliveries continue in martime areas as families in Yasawa and Cikobia face shortages
item.description: Families facing water shortages in the Yasawa Group and Cikobia will continue to receive emergency water supplies as authorities work to assist affected communities in the maritime areas. The National Disaster Risk Management Office says water deliveries, which began last week, will continue in both maritime areas.
item.content:encoded:
Families facing water shortages in the Yasawa Group and Cikobia will continue to receive emergency water supplies as authorities work to assist affected communities in the maritime areas.

The National Disaster Risk Management Office says water deliveries, which began last week, will continue in both maritime areas.

In the Western Division, the MLC Vunilagi will continue delivering water to affected communities in the Yasawa Group, while the vessel MLC Vatulawa will continue delivering emergency water supplies to residents in Cikobia in the Northern Division.

The NDRMO says the operations are being carried out in collaboration with the Ministry of Public Works, Meteorological Services and Transport, the Water Authority of Fiji and other agencies.

They say water deliveries will continue based on the needs of affected communities and weather conditions.

Residents are also urged to conserve water and use their available supplies wisely.

The NDRMO says it will continue monitoring the situation and providing further updates.

item.title: Fiji-linked author honours late Nani through debut children's book, urges people to value their grandparents
item.description: Sheryl Prakash, who has links to Fiji, is encouraging people to value their grandparents, listen to their stories and learn from their experiences while they are still alive, so they do not have regrets later in life. Speaking to fijivillage News from Malaysia, Prakash says her debut children's picture book, The Curry Leaf Tree, was inspired by her late Nani, who played an important role in keepin
item.content:encoded:
Sheryl Prakash, who has links to Fiji, is encouraging people to value their grandparents, listen to their stories and learn from their experiences while they are still alive, so they do not have regrets later in life.

Speaking to fijivillage News from Malaysia, Prakash says her debut children's picture book, The Curry Leaf Tree, was inspired by her late Nani, who played an important role in keeping her connected to her Indo-Fijian heritage.

Born and raised in New Zealand and now living in Malaysia, Prakash says growing up between different cultures was not always easy, as she often struggled to find a sense of belonging.

She says despite coming from a family with a rich cultural background, she sometimes found it difficult to understand where she fits in.

Prakash says her Nani played an important role in teaching her about her family's traditions, values and cultural identity.

Following her Nani's passing in August 2025, Prakash wanted to honour her memory and preserve the lessons and family history she had passed down.

This inspired her to write The Curry Leaf Tree, which reflects her family's journey from India to Fiji and eventually to New Zealand.

Prakash says the book is more than just a children's story, as it highlights the important role grandparents, particularly grandmothers, play in passing down culture, traditions and family values to younger generations.

She says her experience also reflects the challenges faced by Indo-Fijians growing up outside Fiji, particularly when trying to maintain their cultural identity while adapting to life in another country.

As a first-time independent author, Prakash hopes her book will encourage children and families to appreciate their roots and understand the sacrifices and experiences of previous generations.

She stresses that people should spend time with their grandparents, listen to their stories and learn as much as possible from them while they have the opportunity.

Prakash also acknowledges her husband's support and encouragement in helping her turn what started as an idea in 2022 into her first published book.

item.title: More than a crown, Lami Parish pageant gives young people a voice on social issues
item.description: The Immaculate Conception Parish in Lami is using its annual bazaar pageant to give young people a platform to speak out about social issues affecting their lives, including drugs, teenage pregnancy, broken families and cybercrime. Assistant Priest Father Aisea Muaivesi says these are some of the challenges affecting young people in Lami, and the parish wants to give them the confidence to stand u
item.content:encoded:
The Immaculate Conception Parish in Lami is using its annual bazaar pageant to give young people a platform to speak out about social issues affecting their lives, including drugs, teenage pregnancy, broken families and cybercrime.

Assistant Priest Father Aisea Muaivesi says these are some of the challenges affecting young people in Lami, and the parish wants to give them the confidence to stand up and share their views.

He says the pageant was introduced this year not just for beauty or entertainment, but to give young people a voice on issues affecting their communities.

Father Muaivesi says Lami may be a small town, but it has a concentrated population, including families living in settlements such as Qauia, Matata and Valenicina.

He says issues involving drugs, teenage pregnancy, broken families and cybercrime have affected communities in the area over the years.

Father Muaivesi says giving young people an opportunity to speak about these challenges can help them develop the confidence to stand up for themselves and others.

He says when young people share their opinions and concerns, they can become a voice for others facing similar challenges.

Father Muaivesi says another important reason for introducing the pageant was to encourage young women from the parish's five areas to become positive role models.

He says role models are important because young people often follow what they see around them.

Father Muaivesi believes that when young women make positive choices and set a good example, they can help guide younger children towards a better future.

He says the pageant is also an opportunity to encourage more young people to become involved in parish activities.

While the parish already has active youth groups, Father Muaivesi says they want to see more young people participating.

Meanwhile, the Immaculate Conception Parish raised $138,992.16 through its annual bazaar, with funds going towards renovations to the church and parish hall.

Father Muaivesi says the bazaar, which is held only once a year, is also an opportunity to bring families and members of the wider Lami community together.

He says the parish hall is used by members of the public and also generates income for the parish.

He adds that the parish hopes to continue supporting people in need, including the poor and those who are sick, regardless of their religious background.

Father Muaivesi thanked everyone who supported the bazaar, saying coming together and sharing one another's burdens is important in building a stronger community.

The two-day event concluded on Saturday, bringing together the parish's five areas through fundraising and activities aimed at encouraging community and youth participation.

item.title: All races must have equal constitutional rights, Maharaj questions Rabuka's reasons for proposed changes
item.description: The rights of all races must be protected under the Constitution, with a submitter questioning Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka's reasons for the proposed changes during the Constitution Amendment Bill 32 public consultation in Labasa. The submitter, Joytika Maharaj, says Fiji is a multiracial country and the Constitution must protect the rights of every individual, rather than focusing only on the
item.content:encoded:
The rights of all races must be protected under the Constitution, with a submitter questioning Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka's reasons for the proposed changes during the Constitution Amendment Bill 32 public consultation in Labasa.

The submitter, Joytika Maharaj, says Fiji is a multiracial country and the Constitution must protect the rights of every individual, rather than focusing only on the rights of indigenous iTaukei people.

Maharaj questions why Rabuka wants to change the Constitution and says the proposed amendments could be worse than the 2013 Constitution.

She also raises concerns about the treatment of Indo-Fijians, saying comments by some telling Indo Fijians to return to India are disturbing and disrespectful, particularly given the contributions and sacrifices of Girmitiya descendants and their ancestors in building Fiji.

Maharaj says all communities must be treated equally and their contributions to the country must be respected.

She also calls for Fiji to remain a secular state, saying the government and all public office holders must treat every religion equally.

She says the government should not establish Fiji as a Christian state or favour one religion, denomination or belief over another, and all religious groups must be allowed to practise their faith freely.

On land and lease issues, Maharaj says the non-renewal of leases affecting Indo Fijian farmers has forced some farmers to leave their land, affecting their livelihoods and communities.

She says some former sugarcane farms have become overgrown with bush after farmers were unable to continue working their land, resulting in productive agricultural land being left unused.

Maharaj also opposes the inclusion of the Great Council of Chiefs (GCC) in the Constitution, saying the move would waste taxpayers' money.

Insert: Maharaj on interfering in politics 25th Oct 26

She further raises concerns about insufficient time for public input into the constitutional review process, questioning whether people’s submissions will genuinely be considered before any changes are made.

Maharaj also questions the need to return to an earlier system of government, saying this could result in unnecessary public expenditure.

Beyond constitutional issues, Maharaj highlights the lack of basic services in some villages she has visited across Fiji.

She says some communities continue to struggle with access to clean water, proper roads and other essential services.

She has visited iTaukei villages where residents are struggling to access water, with some families unable to wash their children's school uniforms because of the shortage.

She says these challenges show that even the indigenous iTaukei communities continue to face difficulties meeting their basic needs.

Maharaj urges Rabuka and other national leaders to take these concerns into consideration, stressing that the country must address the everyday needs of all communities while ensuring equal rights and protections for everyone.

She says Fiji's future must be built on fairness, respect and equal treatment for all its people.
